Two works use the same arm to evaluate policies. A standardized real-world benchmark reports a taxonomy of failures and recoveries for VLA policies [@2606.08881]. A fleet of SO-101 cells evaluates policies at scale [@2607.24481]. The vla-eval tool runs VLAs across 14 simulation benchmarks [@2603.13966]. A benchmark of demonstration quality studies one method family [@2610.18869]. We test the claims behind methods (judges, world models, latency) against thresholds fixed before the run, and we audit our own pre-registration. RoboSeed [@2610.40026] is the closest work. It scores VLA and world-action models on five dimensions, including reproduction evidence and deployment affordability. Its reproduction-evidence score counts five audit milestones (configuration mapping, task records, task coverage, training records, seeds). Its authors state that this score is not a probability that a result is correct. We give one pass or fail per claim on a €{{rig_eur}} rig.

Two works use the same arm to evaluate policies. One is a standardized real-world benchmark that reports a taxonomy of failures and recoveries for VLA policies [@2606.08881]. The other runs a fleet of SO-101 cells and evaluates policies at scale [@2607.24481]. The vla-eval tool runs VLAs across 14 simulation benchmarks [@2603.13966], and a benchmark of demonstration quality studies one method family [@2610.18869]. We do something different. We test the claims behind methods (judges, world models, latency) against thresholds fixed before the run, and we audit our own pre-registration. The closest work is RoboSeed [@2610.40026]. It scores VLA and world-action models on five dimensions, including reproduction evidence and deployment affordability. The reproduction-evidence score counts five audit milestones: configuration mapping, task records, task coverage, training records and seeds. Its authors state that the score is not a probability that a result is correct. We give one pass or fail per claim on a €{{rig_eur}} rig.

LeWorldModel (LeWM) [@maes2026lewm] trains a world model in two parts. The encoder maps camera frames to a latent vector. The predictor takes the current latent and a sequence of actions and imagines the latents that follow. Both are trained together from pixels with a joint-embedding predictive (JEPA) loss. Papers built on these models propose several uses. Most of them need the predictor. One ranks a policy's candidate action chunks by their imagined outcome. Others flag a failure when the observed latent drifts from the predicted one, read the outcome of a grasp before it happens, or plan over several time scales. Each paper reports the use that worked on its own robot and data.

LeWorldModel [@maes2026lewm] trains the recipe we use end to end from pixels and plans with it in Push-T and in simulation. We tested its two planning uses on our arm, and both fail. LeJEPA's identifiability analysis [@klindt2026lejepa] predicts that SIGReg latents identify the state up to anisotropy. Our pose probes support this in part. DINO-WM [@zhou2024dinowm] plans on frozen DINOv2 [@oquab2023dinov2] patches, and our frozen control uses the same design. We timed V-JEPA 2.1 [@murlabadia2026vjepa21] and RoboJEPA [@zholus2026robojepa] on our on-board computer, and both are too slow. ContactGuard [@zheng2026contactguard] finds imagined-latent probes better than current-latent ones on grasp tasks. On our arm we find the reverse. We also re-tested ReAP's action-conditioned risk [@liu2026reap], the hierarchical planners of HWM [@zhang2026hwm] and H-JEPA [@zhang2026hjepa], and SURVEYOR's latent-distance scale [@surveyor2026]. All of them miss here, at this data scale. SaiVLA-JEPA [@xiao2026saivla] reports that a training-only future-latent head adds {{sai_gain}} points to control on {{sai_eps}} paired episodes. HIJP [@hijp2026] finds LeWM below goal-conditioned behaviour cloning in simulation.
